## 1035 closed (nine tickets); epic 6202's final four stories are unblocked, dispatching SEQUENTIALLY

1035 CLOSED -- 'make verify' is now the documented pre-push contract, and make check's overclaiming
help text is corrected. Thirteen changes merged tonight; nine tickets closed: 3a02, 9a17, c379, 740d,
477b, 09da/S6, 860b, aa40/S1, 1035.

S1 closing unblocked FOUR stories at once: 9183 (S2 docker overlay2), e956 (S3 journald), 2ba3 (S4
/var/tmp), 910b (S5 container layers).

CHECKED FILE OVERLAP BEFORE DISPATCHING, and it changed the plan: ALL FOUR share
infra/scripts/compose-up.sh, infra/scripts/observability.sh,
infra/terraform/monitoring_autodeploy.tf and infra/runbooks/review-bot-ops.md. S2 and S5 additionally
share autodeploy.sh and test_autodeploy_prune.py; S3 and S4 share install-disk-ceilings.sh and
test_observability_disk_pressure.py. So dispatching any two concurrently would guarantee conflicts.
Running them ONE AT A TIME instead.

Started with S2 because it is the largest accumulator and the one with the sharpest trap: the ADR's
census found /var/lib/docker at 17G with overlay2 at 16G across 67 layer directories, while
'docker system df' claimed ~9.5 GB with ZERO dangling images. Roughly 6.5 GB of orphaned overlay2 was
INVISIBLE TO docker prune ENTIRELY. So a cap that trusts Docker's own accounting will not see the
bytes that caused the outage -- I made that the crux of the brief rather than leaving it to be
rediscovered.

Also passed forward the two patterns S1 established, so they are reused rather than reinvented: two
markers on two filesystems (because an unmounted mount point raises NOTHING), and two alarms rather
than one (a generator that failed to start reads 0% used -- perfectly healthy -- while the thing it
feeds is broken; one alarm structurally cannot answer for the other, per the 3e92 precedent). The
ticket's own title says 'per-generator alarms', which is the same principle: alarm on what PRODUCES
the bytes, not only on aggregate fullness.

Told it explicitly to note any shared-file restructuring it deliberately leaves alone, so the next
story can build on it rather than fight it.
